summary: BBN's host status report for February 14 to 25, 1972, noting that MIT-AI became a network user. It was replaced by RFC 319.

plainLanguage.summary: A report on which network computers were up in late February.

questions: how did early networks check if computers were working
what were the first network status reports
subtitle: A snapshot of which ARPANET computers were working in mid-February 1972.

tldr.problem: Early network operators needed to know which computers were available on the ARPANET so they could route traffic and decide where to send jobs.
tldr.mechanism: Ellen Westheimer at BBN ran daily tests of the network, connecting to each host and recording whether it responded, was busy, timed out, or was dead.
tldr.outcome: This report became the first in a series of weekly network status updates that helped ARPANET users stay informed about available resources.

today: RFC 315 is a historic document superseded by RFC 319. It documents one week's snapshot of the early ARPANET's operational state.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC reports on the status of the ARPANET's host computers during the two weeks of February 14 to 25, 1972. During this period, MIT's Artificial Intelligence laboratory at address 134 joined the network as a new user.

The report explains which computers were tested daily and which ones were excluded from testing because they were not yet network servers or were not expected to respond.
sections.plainLanguage: This report is like a checklist of computers on the early network, saying which ones are ready to help and which ones are being worked on.

sections.title: Excluded Hosts
sections.content:
Some hosts were not included in daily testing. The first category included machines expected to be unavailable: MIT-AI (address 134), Case (13), and AMES/Paoli (15). The second category included hosts that were users only, not servers: Terminal IMPs at several sites and the Network Control Center computer (address 5) that gathered statistics.

This distinction mattered for operations: the network did not expect to use these machines to host services for other sites.
sections.plainLanguage: Some machines were like students getting library cards instead of working at the library desk. They were just using the network, not offering a service to others.

sections.title: Test Results
sections.content:
For two weeks, BBN's Terminal IMP tested connectivity to each host multiple times per day. The results used status codes: O (Open: connected and accessible), D (Dead: unreachable), T (Timed out: no response in 60 seconds), H (1/2 Open: connected but then closed immediately).

The report shows that reliability varied widely. Some hosts like UCLA-NMC and MIT-Multics were mostly open, while others like AMES and Stanford-AI were down nearly every day.
sections.plainLanguage: The test used simple letters to show each computer's condition: O meant it was awake and listening, D meant it was off or broken, and H meant it answered but then hung up.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: This RFC was replaced by RFC 319, which continued the weekly network status reporting. Network host status reports became a regular publication throughout the ARPANET era.
sections.plainLanguage: This report was only for two weeks. After that, someone else kept writing similar reports to help network users know which computers were working.

references.text: Westheimer, E., "Network Host Status", RFC 319, March 1972.
